content.name: Pavol Struhár
openTo: joint projects with companies generating high-frequency sensor or telematics data

consulting on Bayesian model design and validation
student internships for data science and statistics students

bio.text: Pavol Struhár completed his undergraduate studies in Mathematics at the University of Novi Sad in 2008 and received his PhD in Applied Mathematics from the same institution in 2014, with a dissertation on Bayesian change-point detection in non-stationary time series. He held a postdoctoral position at the University of Ljubljana (2015–2017) before returning to Novi Sad as an Assistant Professor in the Department of Mathematics and Informatics. His group works on statistical methods for high-frequency IoT sensor data, covering feature extraction pipelines, extreme-value theory for rare failure events, and Bayesian models for individualised actuarial pricing in insurance and maintenance contexts. He teaches probability theory, stochastic processes, and statistical computing. The group uses a small cluster of GPU workstations and has access to streaming data infrastructure shared with the Faculty of Technical Sciences.

industryExperience.text: During 2019–2020, Struhár provided statistical consulting to a regional property insurer on the design of a sensor-based premium adjustment scheme for commercial fire risk, covering model specification, data pipeline requirements, and regulatory documentation. He has also collaborated informally with an automotive components supplier in the context of a feature extraction benchmarking study.

notes.text: Struhár is currently supervising two PhD students and has capacity for one further industrial PhD candidate starting from the 2025–2026 academic year. He prefers collaborations where data-sharing agreements can be established formally; his department has a standard template for this. He is not on sabbatical and has no planned leave through 2027.

works.title: Bayesian Change-Point Detection in Non-Stationary Industrial Time Series

body.text: This paper addresses the identification of abrupt structural changes in time series generated by industrial sensors operating at sampling rates between 10 Hz and 100 Hz. A Bayesian online algorithm based on a product-partition model is adapted to handle autocorrelated noise and missing observations, which are common in factory-floor deployments. The method was evaluated on 14 months of vibration data from three manufacturing sites in central Serbia, comprising approximately 2.1 billion data points. Posterior inference was carried out using a Rao–Blackwellised particle filter, with run-time profiling showing the algorithm processes a 100 Hz stream in under 8 milliseconds per sample on standard server hardware. Against a ground-truth log of 47 documented equipment incidents, the approach achieved a detection rate of 91.5% with a median latency of 1.3 seconds. A comparison with CUSUM and PELT baselines shows consistent improvement in false-positive rate at fixed recall. Model hyperparameters were set via empirical Bayes using an initial 30-day warm-up period.

works.title: Feature Extraction Benchmarks for Multivariate Sensor Streams in Predictive Maintenance

body.text: A systematic comparison of 22 feature extraction approaches is presented for multivariate time-series data from rotating machinery. Feature families evaluated include statistical moments, entropy-based descriptors, wavelet sub-band energies, and autoregressive coefficients, each extracted over sliding windows of 0.5 s, 1 s, and 5 s. Experiments used publicly available bearing datasets supplemented by proprietary vibration logs from a Serbian automotive components supplier, totalling roughly 650 hours of continuous recording across six sensor channels. Features were fed into random forest and gradient-boosted classifiers. Wavelet sub-band energy features consistently ranked highest by mutual information with failure labels, and combining them with sample entropy yielded the best downstream F1 score of 0.88 on held-out data. Computational cost per feature family is reported in CPU-seconds, providing guidance for real-time deployment choices. The paper also proposes a simple dimensionality reduction step that retains 95% of predictive power while cutting feature dimensionality by a factor of four.

works.title: Hierarchical Bayesian Models for Failure Rate Heterogeneity Across Machine Populations

body.text: Industrial fleets of nominally identical machines exhibit substantial heterogeneity in failure rates even after controlling for operating conditions. This paper develops a hierarchical Bayesian Poisson–Gamma model for failure counts observed over irregular inspection intervals, allowing partial pooling of information across 312 compressor units monitored over three years at a natural gas distribution company. A Markov chain Monte Carlo sampler (No-U-Turn) was used for posterior estimation; convergence was verified via Gelman–Rubin diagnostics on 4 independent chains. Unit-level posterior failure rate estimates had a coefficient of variation of 0.34, confirming meaningful heterogeneity. Predictive posterior distributions for time to next failure were used to rank units by expected residual life, and a field trial showed that prioritising the bottom 20% of units by posterior mean life reduced unplanned outages by 31% compared to the previous calendar-based schedule. The sensitivity of results to prior hyperparameter choice is discussed, and a weakly informative default prior is recommended.

works.title: Extreme-Value Modelling of Pressure Spike Amplitudes in Water Distribution Networks

body.text: Transient pressure spikes in water distribution networks can cause pipe fatigue and burst failures. This study fits generalised extreme-value (GEV) distributions to block maxima of pressure readings collected at 4 Hz from 28 monitoring nodes across the Novi Sad municipal network over 26 months. Block sizes of one week and one month are compared; likelihood ratio tests favour weekly blocks for this dataset. Maximum likelihood estimates indicate heavy-tailed behaviour (shape parameter ξ̂ ranging from 0.11 to 0.29 across nodes) that is inconsistent with Gaussian or exponential tail assumptions used in standard hydraulic standards. Return-level estimates at 10-year and 50-year periods are reported with 95% profile-likelihood confidence intervals. A spatial analysis using a max-stable process model reveals a correlation range of approximately 2.1 km, meaning that simultaneous extreme events at nodes within this distance must be treated as dependent. The results inform updated inspection intervals recommended to the municipal utility.

works.title: Individualised Actuarial Pricing Using Telematics Features: A Credibility Theory Perspective

body.text: Usage-based insurance pricing has shifted from simple mileage adjustments to models that incorporate behavioural features extracted from vehicle telematics. This paper re-examines the problem through the lens of Bühlmann–Straub credibility theory, showing that classic credibility estimators can be embedded in a Bayesian linear model with conjugate normal–inverse-gamma priors. Trip-level feature vectors (hard-braking rate, speed percentiles, time-of-day distribution, cornering events) were derived from 1 Hz GPS and accelerometer streams of 4,200 policyholders over 12 months, yielding approximately 18 million trip records. The credibility-weighted premium estimator reduced the mean squared prediction error of claim costs by 14.2% relative to a market-segment flat rate and by 6.8% relative to a generalised linear model with the same features but no credibility adjustment. The paper discusses regulatory constraints on feature selection under Serbian and EU insurance law and outlines a procedure for updating the model quarterly as new data arrive.

works.title: Online Variational Inference for Streaming Sensor Anomaly Detection

body.text: Batch Bayesian inference is impractical when sensor streams arrive continuously and model parameters must be updated in near real time. This paper investigates stochastic variational inference (SVI) as an online alternative, using a Gaussian mixture likelihood with a Dirichlet process prior to model the multimodal distribution of normal operating states. The algorithm processes mini-batches of 500 observations drawn from four temperature and humidity sensors on a cold-chain logistics platform, with one parameter update per second. On a 90-day evaluation dataset with 63 labelled anomaly episodes (ranging from 4 minutes to 11 hours), the SVI approach reached an area under the ROC curve of 0.93, compared to 0.89 for a static trained model retrained nightly. Memory footprint was 12 MB for the variational parameters, making the method deployable on edge devices with modest RAM. Drift in the variational posterior over time is characterised and a forgetting factor mechanism is proposed to prevent stale components from dominating.

works.title: Risk Scoring for Agricultural IoT Networks Under Sparse and Irregular Sampling

body.text: Soil moisture, leaf wetness, and microclimate sensors deployed across vineyards in Fruška Gora are sampled irregularly owing to energy-harvesting constraints, yielding gaps that can span several days. This paper adapts a Gaussian process regression framework to reconstruct latent continuous processes from irregular observations and derives a composite risk score for fungal disease onset. The GP kernel is chosen by leave-one-vineyard-out cross-validation among Matérn 3/2, squared-exponential, and rational-quadratic families; Matérn 3/2 was selected in 11 of 14 vineyard sites. Risk score thresholds calibrated to achieve 85% sensitivity for disease onset predicted spray interventions 2.1 days earlier on average than the standard phenological calendar used by local agronomists, over three growing seasons across 14 sites. A cost-benefit analysis using spray cost and expected yield loss figures from local agricultural records shows a mean saving of approximately 310 EUR per hectare per season under the model-guided schedule.

works.title: Probabilistic Load Forecasting for Small Industrial Consumers Using Meter Data and Bayesian Quantile Regression

body.text: Short-term electricity load forecasting for small and medium industrial consumers is more difficult than for large sites owing to high variability relative to mean demand. This study uses 15-minute smart meter readings from 87 SME customers of a regional distribution company in Vojvodina, covering 28 months. A Bayesian quantile regression model is fitted for each customer, with temperature, hour-of-day, day-of-week, and a 5-lag autoregressive component as covariates. Posterior predictive intervals at the 10th, 50th, and 90th quantiles are evaluated using the pinball loss and empirical coverage. Compared to a pooled point-forecast baseline, the per-customer Bayesian model reduces pinball loss by a median of 18% and achieves nominal coverage within 2 percentage points for 81 of 87 customers. The paper discusses practical aspects of deploying the model in a metering data management system, including re-estimation frequency and handling of customers with fewer than six months of history.

works.title: A Survey of Bayesian Methods for IoT-Driven Actuarial Modelling

body.text: This survey reviews 15 years of literature at the intersection of Bayesian statistics, IoT sensor data, and actuarial modelling, covering approximately 140 papers published between 2009 and 2024. The scope includes telematics-based motor insurance, sensor-monitored property insurance, maintenance-linked warranty pricing, and health wearable applications. The review is organised around four modelling tasks: hazard rate estimation, claims severity modelling, experience rating, and catastrophe risk quantification. For each task, the survey describes the predominant likelihood structures, prior specification strategies, and computational approaches. Key findings include a shift from conjugate analytical solutions to variational and sequential Monte Carlo methods after 2018, driven by data volume growth, and a persistent gap between academic model complexity and insurer implementation capacity. The paper identifies open problems in non-stationarity handling, regulatory interpretability requirements, and cross-domain transfer of fitted models as priorities for future research.

works.title: Sequential Bayesian Updating of Remaining Useful Life Distributions Under Concept Drift

body.text: Remaining useful life (RUL) models for rotating equipment are typically trained once and then applied statically, but operating conditions and load profiles drift over months or years, causing predictive accuracy to degrade. This preprint proposes a sequential Bayesian updating scheme in which the posterior over RUL model parameters is revised each time a failure or censoring event is recorded, using an importance-weighted likelihood that down-weights observations older than a tunable half-life τ. The method is evaluated on three datasets: a benchmark turbofan engine simulation, a set of 41 conveyor belt drives monitored over 31 months, and compressor units from a previous study by the same group. Choosing τ by cross-validation over a held-out cohort reduced mean absolute RUL error by 22% compared to the static model and by 9% compared to periodic full re-fitting on a 90-day rolling window. Computational overhead relative to a static model is approximately 3% per update cycle.

works.title: Piecewise-Linear Approximation of ECG Signals Using Adaptive Breakpoint Selection

body.text: This paper examines piecewise-linear approximation as a preprocessing stage for ECG compression. A dynamic-programming algorithm selects breakpoints by minimising the sum of squared residuals subject to a maximum reconstruction error bound of 10 µV. Experiments were conducted on 30 records from the PhysioNet MIT-BIH arrhythmia database resampled to 360 Hz. The method achieves an average compression ratio of 4.1:1 at a per-sample root-mean-square error below 8 µV, outperforming fixed-window linear interpolation by approximately 18% in bit rate under identical distortion constraints. Computational cost is O(N log N) per record, making the approach suitable for microcontroller deployment in wearable monitors. The study also evaluates how premature ventricular contractions, which deviate from normal quasi-periodic morphology, affect the breakpoint density and proposes a beat-classification pre-filter that reduces the density penalty for irregular beats by 23%.

works.title: Evaluating Explanation Fidelity Under Prompt Variation in Instruction-Tuned Language Models

body.text: Instruction-tuned language models can produce natural-language explanations for their own outputs on request, but it is unclear whether these self-explanations reflect the model's actual inference path or are generated independently of it. This paper measures explanation fidelity by comparing self-generated explanations to three external explanation methods (saliency, attention rollout, and a perturbation-based method) across 600 prompted classification and extraction tasks. Agreement between self-explanations and external methods, measured by normalised token-level overlap, averages 0.41 and varies substantially with prompt wording. Systematically varying the explanation prompt reveals that adding the phrase 'cite the exact words from the input that determined your answer' raises agreement to 0.55 without affecting task performance. We also find that self-explanations are more likely to be faithful when the model's output confidence is high and when the task is extractive rather than abstractive. The results have practical implications for the design of explanation prompts in deployed systems and suggest that external verification of self-explanations is necessary for high-stakes applications.

works.title: Grammar Inference from Domain Equations to Bootstrap Symbolic Regression Constraints

body.text: When domain equations are partially known, the information they contain can be used to infer a context-free grammar that guides symbolic regression toward physically meaningful solutions. This work proposes a two-stage pipeline: first, a small set of validated domain equations is used to extract production rules via a rule-mining procedure based on frequent subtree enumeration; second, the resulting grammar seeds the hypothesis space for grammar-guided genetic programming. The approach is evaluated on problems from process engineering and soil mechanics, where partial knowledge of governing equations exists. On six benchmark problems with 150–600 data points, the bootstrapped grammar recovers correct functional forms in 83% of runs compared with 51% for uninformed grammar-guided GP and 44% for standard GP. A sensitivity analysis shows performance degrades gracefully when the seed equations contain up to 30% incorrect terms, making the method robust to imperfect domain knowledge.

works.title: Sensor-Driven Probabilistic Risk Models for SME Asset Management

body.text: The project developed a modular software pipeline for ingesting high-frequency IoT sensor streams, extracting interpretable statistical features, and fitting hierarchical Bayesian risk models suitable for small and medium enterprises that lack dedicated data science teams. Use cases were developed in collaboration with three SMEs in Vojvodina operating in food processing, cold-chain logistics, and metal fabrication. A reference implementation was released as open-source software. The project supported two PhD students and produced eight peer-reviewed outputs. A key output was a calibration protocol that allows a new site to obtain reliable risk scores after as little as 60 days of sensor history by borrowing strength from previously observed sites via the hierarchical model structure.

works.title: Statistical Modelling for Precision Agriculture Sensor Networks in the Pannonian Region

body.text: A cross-border project linking agricultural research stations in Vojvodina and southern Hungary to develop statistical models for disease risk, irrigation need, and microclimate characterisation from low-power IoT sensor grids. Struhár leads the work package on probabilistic modelling and uncertainty quantification, contributing Gaussian process and Bayesian hierarchical methods tailored to irregular and energy-constrained sampling schedules. The project deploys sensor networks across 28 partner farms and two experimental stations. Expected outputs include operational decision-support tools, a joint training programme for agronomists, and at least 12 scientific publications. The project runs alongside the research group's existing vineyard collaboration and extends it to wheat, sunflower, and paprika cultivation.
